The board should treat nuclear fuel risk as a manageable procurement and geopolitical issue, not as an automatic deal-breaker, provided the contract covers the whole fuel chain rather than merely “uranium.” The chain is mining and milling, conversion of yellowcake into uranium hexafluoride, enrichment, fabrication of reactor fuel, transport, and finally an inventory held before loading. Mining risk is real because reactor demand can exceed current mine output, and secondary supplies such as utility inventories, government stocks, recycled fuel, and weapons-derived material have historically filled the gap. The important implication is that a mine disruption usually does not stop a reactor immediately, because plants commonly hold roughly five to seven years of fuel inventory, but it can create a future contracting and price problem if inventories are being drawn down. Kazakhstan matters chiefly as a large mining source, but production there is exposed to practical operating dependencies such as sulfuric-acid availability, piping, and the difficulty of ramping output reliably, not just to the political stability of the country. China matters both because it is building nuclear capacity and because Chinese utilities have sought greater control of their own uranium resources, while reported Chinese utility inventories have been substantial. The more easily overlooked bottleneck is midstream capacity: conversion is needed to make UF6 for enrichment, enrichment capacity is specialized and concentrated, and fabrication must turn enriched material into qualified pellets, fuel pins, and assemblies that match the reactor design. A conversion outage or enrichment constraint can therefore matter even when uranium ore is plentiful, and recent market commentary reported conversion prices rising from about $4 to more than $40 per kilogram and enrichment prices from roughly $35–40 to more than $140 per separative-work unit. Russian exposure is consequently broader than buying Russian ore: Russia has historically operated significant conversion and enrichment facilities, and its fuel-cycle assets are associated with Rosatom and TVEL. The right response is not simply to prohibit Russian-origin uranium, but to require the supplier to disclose origin and ownership at every stage, cap Russian and single-country exposure, maintain qualified non-Russian conversion and enrichment alternatives, and demonstrate that those alternatives can actually deliver fuel compatible with the plant. For a conventional reactor, the board should distinguish uranium-price risk from fuel-availability risk: uranium is a relatively small component of total nuclear generating cost, so an ore-price spike is more likely to affect the supplier’s economics and future contract price than to cause an immediate large increase in the power-purchase price. Price risk nevertheless matters because spot uranium is a small part of the physical market, while most reactor purchases are made under term contracts, and spot prices can still signal scarcity and pull long-term prices upward. A long-term contract protects a utility against some price volatility and gives producers a reason to finance mines and capacity, but it does not by itself guarantee delivery if the contract depends on one mine, one converter, one enricher, one fabricator, or a supplier whose parent company becomes sanctioned or insolvent. The PPA should therefore make fuel security a measurable obligation by specifying minimum years of forward fuel coverage, multiple qualified suppliers for each stage, limits on Russian and other politically exposed content, rights to substitute equivalent material, supplier-held strategic inventory, delivery deadlines, penalties, and transparent pass-through rules for uranium, conversion, enrichment, fabrication, transport, and hedging costs. The procurement team should ask for a “fuel availability case” showing the reactor’s annual requirements, the exact origin and contractual status of each stage, inventory at each stage, alternative routes after a disruption, and the time required to qualify a replacement supplier, because retaining two or three suppliers for each stage is a more meaningful protection than having several names on a uranium-mining list. HALEU changes the assessment for a possible advanced reactor: it is uranium enriched above 5% and below 20% uranium-235, it is not yet broadly commercially available, and the evidence retrieved identifies Russia and China as having production infrastructure at scale while US production was only at demonstration scale in the cited period. An SMR or advanced-reactor option should therefore not be approved on the assumption that ordinary light-water-reactor fuel contracting will carry over, but only after the vendor identifies a licensed HALEU supplier, conversion and enrichment route, fuel-fabrication facility, inventory plan, and credible non-Russian backup. The board should treat nuclear fuel risk as a manageable procurement and geopolitical issue, not as an automatic deal-breaker, provided the contract covers the whole fuel chain rather than merely “uranium.” [shard_04067_14360] [shard_05719_30310]

The chain is mining and milling, conversion of yellowcake into uranium hexafluoride, enrichment, fabrication of reactor fuel, transport, and finally an inventory held before loading. [shard_04067_14360] [shard_01382_7039]

Mining risk is real because reactor demand can exceed current mine output, and secondary supplies such as utility inventories, government stocks, recycled fuel, and weapons-derived material have historically filled the gap. [shard_01854_75617] [shard_04841_81396]

The important implication is that a mine disruption usually does not stop a reactor immediately, because plants commonly hold roughly five to seven years of fuel inventory, but it can create a future contracting and price problem if inventories are being drawn down. [shard_02551_52575] [shard_03216_10146]

Kazakhstan matters chiefly as a large mining source, but production there is exposed to practical operating dependencies such as sulfuric-acid availability, piping, and the difficulty of ramping output reliably, not just to the political stability of the country. [shard_01904_19426]

China matters both because it is building nuclear capacity and because Chinese utilities have sought greater control of their own uranium resources, while reported Chinese utility inventories have been substantial. [shard_05112_59357] [shard_05480_7160]

The more easily overlooked bottleneck is midstream capacity: conversion is needed to make UF6 for enrichment, enrichment capacity is specialized and concentrated, and fabrication must turn enriched material into qualified pellets, fuel pins, and assemblies that match the reactor design. [shard_03205_15916] [shard_01382_7039]

A conversion outage or enrichment constraint can therefore matter even when uranium ore is plentiful, and recent market commentary reported conversion prices rising from about $4 to more than $40 per kilogram and enrichment prices from roughly $35–40 to more than $140 per separative-work unit. [shard_01504_57750]

Russian exposure is consequently broader than buying Russian ore: Russia has historically operated significant conversion and enrichment facilities, and its fuel-cycle assets are associated with Rosatom and TVEL. [shard_03247_71868]

The right response is not simply to prohibit Russian-origin uranium, but to require the supplier to disclose origin and ownership at every stage, cap Russian and single-country exposure, maintain qualified non-Russian conversion and enrichment alternatives, and demonstrate that those alternatives can actually deliver fuel compatible with the plant. [shard_03247_71868] [shard_01049_70993]

For a conventional reactor, the board should distinguish uranium-price risk from fuel-availability risk: uranium is a relatively small component of total nuclear generating cost, so an ore-price spike is more likely to affect the supplier’s economics and future contract price than to cause an immediate large increase in the power-purchase price. [shard_06088_69156] [shard_06087_427]

Price risk nevertheless matters because spot uranium is a small part of the physical market, while most reactor purchases are made under term contracts, and spot prices can still signal scarcity and pull long-term prices upward. [shard_03242_80346] [shard_01504_57750]

A long-term contract protects a utility against some price volatility and gives producers a reason to finance mines and capacity, but it does not by itself guarantee delivery if the contract depends on one mine, one converter, one enricher, one fabricator, or a supplier whose parent company becomes sanctioned or insolvent. [shard_01868_5915] [shard_03216_10146]

The PPA should therefore make fuel security a measurable obligation by specifying minimum years of forward fuel coverage, multiple qualified suppliers for each stage, limits on Russian and other politically exposed content, rights to substitute equivalent material, supplier-held strategic inventory, delivery deadlines, penalties, and transparent pass-through rules for uranium, conversion, enrichment, fabrication, transport, and hedging costs. [shard_05719_30310] [shard_01868_5915]

The procurement team should ask for a “fuel availability case” showing the reactor’s annual requirements, the exact origin and contractual status of each stage, inventory at each stage, alternative routes after a disruption, and the time required to qualify a replacement supplier, because retaining two or three suppliers for each stage is a more meaningful protection than having several names on a uranium-mining list. [shard_05719_30310]

HALEU changes the assessment for a possible advanced reactor: it is uranium enriched above 5% and below 20% uranium-235, it is not yet broadly commercially available, and the evidence retrieved identifies Russia and China as having production infrastructure at scale while US production was only at demonstration scale in the cited period. [shard_00511_50062]

An SMR or advanced-reactor option should therefore not be approved on the assumption that ordinary light-water-reactor fuel contracting will carry over, but only after the vendor identifies a licensed HALEU supplier, conversion and enrichment route, fuel-fabrication facility, inventory plan, and credible non-Russian backup. [shard_00511_50062] [shard_01382_7039]

The board’s decision rule should be that conventional nuclear fuel risk is acceptable when the project has years of inventory, diversified stage-by-stage contracts, non-Russian qualified alternatives, and a supplier-backed contingency plan, whereas an unqualified HALEU supply chain or a contract that merely promises “uranium supply” should be treated as a material project risk.
